text: HashMap lookup pattern: when you need to find a complement, pair, or previously seen value in O(1), store values in a HashMap as you iterate. Check existence before inserting. Problems: Two Sum, Four Sum, Subarray Sum equals K, Group Anagrams.

Two Pointers pattern: use when array is sorted or you need to find a pair. Place one pointer at start, one at end. Move them toward each other based on condition. Problems: Two Sum II, Container With Most Water, 3Sum, Trapping Rain Water.

Sliding Window pattern: use for subarrays or substrings of variable or fixed size. Expand right pointer, shrink left pointer when condition breaks. Use a set or map to track window contents. Problems: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters, Max Sum Subarray, Minimum Window Substring.

Fast and Slow Pointers pattern: use to detect cycles in linked lists or arrays. Fast pointer moves 2 steps, slow moves 1. They meet if a cycle exists. Problems: Linked List Cycle, Find Duplicate Number, Middle of Linked List.

Binary Search pattern: use when array is sorted or search space can be halved. Maintain low and high pointers. Move mid based on condition. Problems: Search in Rotated Sorted Array, Find Minimum in Rotated Array, Koko Eating Bananas.

1D Dynamic Programming pattern: use when problem has overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure. Define dp[i] as answer for subproblem i. Build up from base case. Problems: Climbing Stairs, House Robber, Coin Change, Longest Increasing Subsequence.

2D Dynamic Programming pattern: use for grid problems or string comparison. Define dp[i][j] as answer for subproblem at row i col j. Problems: Unique Paths, Longest Common Subsequence, Edit Distance, Coin Change 2.

BFS Breadth First Search pattern: use for shortest path in unweighted graph or level order traversal. Use a queue. Process level by level. Problems: Binary Tree Level Order, Shortest Path in Binary Matrix, Word Ladder, Rotting Oranges.

DFS Depth First Search pattern: use for exploring all paths, connected components, or tree traversal. Use recursion or explicit stack. Mark visited nodes. Problems: Number of Islands, Clone Graph, Path Sum, All Paths Source to Target.

Backtracking pattern: use for generating all combinations, permutations, or subsets. Make a choice, recurse, then undo the choice. Prune branches early when constraint is violated. Problems: Subsets, Permutations, Combination Sum, N-Queens, Sudoku Solver.

Monotonic Stack pattern: use when you need next greater or smaller element. Maintain a stack that is always increasing or decreasing. Pop when current element breaks the order. Problems: Daily Temperatures, Largest Rectangle in Histogram, Next Greater Element.

Heap Top K pattern: use when you need the K largest or smallest elements. Use a min-heap of size K for K largest, max-heap for K smallest. Problems: Kth Largest Element, Top K Frequent Elements, K Closest Points to Origin.

Merge Intervals pattern: sort intervals by start time. Compare each interval with the last merged one. If they overlap, extend the end. Problems: Merge Intervals, Insert Interval, Meeting Rooms, Non-overlapping Intervals.

Trie prefix tree pattern: use for problems involving prefix search or word dictionaries. Each node has children map and isEnd flag. Insert and search by traversing character by character. Problems: Implement Trie, Word Search II, Replace Words.

Union Find Disjoint Set pattern: use for grouping elements into connected components. Maintain parent array. Find root with path compression. Union by rank. Problems: Number of Connected Components, Redundant Connection, Accounts Merge.
